clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive immuno-osseous dysplasia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ACP5, which encodes tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP).
Also classified as a monogenic type I interferonopathy, which accounts for the prominent autoimmunity and intracranial calcification.
The skeletal hallmark is platyspondyly with metaphyseal and vertebral radiolucent lesions representing islands of ectopic cartilage, causing disproportionate short stature and spinal deformity.
Neurological features include spasticity, developmental delay, cognitive impairment and basal ganglia calcification.
Immune dysregulation is common, with systemic lupus erythematosus, autoimmune thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia and thyroiditis, alongside variable susceptibility to infection.
Deficient TRAP activity leads to accumulation of phosphorylated osteopontin, mechanistically linking the bone and immune phenotypes.
A raised blood interferon signature supports the diagnosis.
The radiolucent skeletal lesions are not true enchondromas and should not be mistaken for Ollier disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Spondyloenchondrodysplasia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in ACP5, encoding tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), an enzyme expressed in osteoclasts, dendritic cells and macrophages. TRAP normally dephosphorylates osteopontin, a phosphoprotein that regulates bone mineralisation and remodelling and modulates immune-cell activation. Loss of TRAP activity leads to accumulation of the highly phosphorylated form of osteopontin, disturbing the coordinated activity of osteoclasts and chondrocytes so that persistent islands of cartilage remain within the metaphyses and vertebrae, producing the enchondromatous, platyspondylic skeletal phenotype. In parallel, dysregulated osteopontin signalling and a dominant type I interferon response drive loss of self-tolerance, autoantibody production and intracranial calcification, accounting for the coexistent lupus-like autoimmunity, cytopenias and progressive neurological disease that characterise the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome (true enchondromatosis)
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome (intracranial calcification with interferon signature)
Systemic lupus erythematosus of other cause
Metabolic bone disease with metaphyseal changes such as rickets
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating platyspondyly with metaphyseal and vertebral lucencies
Molecular genetic testing for ACP5 variants
Neuroimaging for basal ganglia and other intracranial calcification
Autoantibody panel including ANA and anti-dsDNA with a direct antiglobulin test
Full blood count to detect autoimmune cytopenias
redFlags: Severe autoimmune cytopenias such as thrombocytopenia or haemolytic anaemia
Lupus nephritis or other major organ autoimmunity
Progressive neurological deterioration or worsening spasticity
Serious or recurrent infection suggesting associated immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on the severity of autoimmune and neurological involvement. Skeletal disease causes short stature and spinal deformity, while lupus-like autoimmunity and progressive neurological impairment drive long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the enchondroma-like lesions as Ollier disease.
Diagnosing isolated systemic lupus erythematosus and missing the underlying monogenic cause.
Overlooking intracranial calcification as an incidental finding.
Attributing the short stature to a non-syndromic skeletal dysplasia.
